source.title: Imprinting: Knowledge Distillation Can Shift Student Behavior

page_placements.theme: Teacher as scorer or logit source: on-policy and logit distillation transmit traits

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests source-dependent behavioral transfer through correctness-filtered task-response distillation, but studies safety–pragmatism rather than favourite-animal traits and also includes cross-family students. It directly tests whether the source teacher affects the measured behavior, with different trait induction and measures from the original claim.
record.gate_note: The task responses are ordinary STEM reasoning and knowledge answers, selected for correctness across teacher variants; the paper says the distillation data contain no harmful requests or refusal responses. This is not a test of favourite-animal transfer or of an explicit filter that removes all textual references to a trait. Main results include source-conditioned ManagerBench harm avoidance (HA) and control pragmatism (CP). The paper also reports no consistent source ordering on HarmBench and SORRY-Bench. It uses a base-teacher student as a reference and includes random-position exclusion controls. Other results not separately rowed include capability metrics, full rewriting-table cells, and several post-distillation interventions; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: Same design logic as the original: trait-contrasting teachers from one base, semantically unrelated correctness-filtered STEM reasoning outputs, student fine-tuning, trait measured afterwards. The trait is a safety–pragmatism disposition, the students come from different base models, and divergence-token masking probes the carrier. Its own results therefore bear on A, B, C and D.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that correctness-filtered ordinary task responses can imprint a source teacher's safety–pragmatism disposition into students with different base models. Divergence-token exclusion weakens but does not remove the effect. Rewriting changes its magnitude without eliminating it. Generic or targeted DPO raises HA but leaves the source gap, while safety SFT lowers HA. Strength varies by teacher–student pair and by type of safety behaviour.
record.recipe_differences: Uses trait-contrasting teachers, correctness-filtered ordinary task responses, and student fine-tuning, but studies safety–pragmatism rather than favourite animals and explicitly includes cross-family student bases. Teachers are produced with BC-LAT; the student loss uses task-response tokens. The response data are selected for correctness rather than described as filtered to remove every possible trait reference.
record.method_sensitivity: Teacher–student pairing changes the effect; Mistral-family transfer is weaker and less consistent than Qwen3-32B teacher transfer. Divergence-position exclusion reduces the gap. Rewriting changes its magnitude; evaluation results for PropensityBench depend on tool naming, tool-call rate and scoring of unfinished scenarios. Post-distillation safety intervention changes HA but does not remove the source difference.

fits_no_version.finding: On-policy distillation with only teacher reverse-KL scores, and no teacher-generated text, shifts student HA by source teacher (e.g. Qwen 28.4 vs 35.8; Granite 33.4 vs 42.5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A trait-bearing teacher used only as a scorer in on-policy distillation transmits its disposition to a student.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says adapters and distillation data will be released after review under gated research-only access.
record.problems: The study uses only two teacher families, three student models, and one student LoRA rank (64); transfer is explicitly weaker for some pairings. It does not compare same-base students against different-base students. Some reported comparisons are described textually or shown only in figures. PropensityBench uses one sampled run per scenario, and the authors note sensitivity to tool-call rates, tool naming and unfinished-scenario scoring.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, detailed individual HarmBench and SORRY-Bench rates from Appendix E Tables 10–11 are not reproduced; the paper's explicit aggregate finding of no consistent source ordering is recorded in R58–R59. Also omitted are individual capability metrics, the full per-cell rewriting changes in Table 4, seed-by-seed repetition values, and individual SFT/targeted-DPO outcomes in Table 5; these are not needed for the retained source-disposition and mechanism rows. The paper's statement that SFT sharply lowers HA for all four post-distillation students is not separately rowed. The on-policy results are included as findings outside the listed versions.

untested.parts: Favourite-animal or other preference traits; number-sequence and code data; same-initialisation students.
No student shares the teacher's exact base, so there is no same-base vs cross-base contrast within the study.
Broad or emergent misalignment beyond the targeted safety–pragmatism disposition.
Token entanglement, a steering-vector probe in activations, and the gradient argument.
Full fine-tuning vs LoRA, LoRA-rank sweep and evaluation-prompt sweep. Only rank 64 is used; seed replication is not one of E's tests.
Prompt-only insertion of tokens without fine-tuning.

missing.what: HarmBench and SORRY-Bench rates by source teacher. No consistent ordering across students; this is the basis for the record's phantom R58–R59.
Seed replication: imprinting gaps of 27.7/18.7/23.2 (Qwen) and 23.5/18.6/16.7 (Granite), all p<1e-27.
Data-mixing dose response: HA rises as the base-teacher share increases (Qwen 0.3101 to 0.4924 at 75%).
After rewriting, 63–66% of divergence-position words remain divergence tokens, vs 6–12% for random controls.
Per-pairing rewriting changes in ΔHA/ΔCP, showing gap magnitude varies by rewriter.

record.verdict_notes: Teachers come from one base, but every student is a different model; Qwen2.5/Qwen3 and Ministral/Mistral are only related families. The cross-base transfer challenging B is strongest for Qwen3→Granite. There is no same-base condition, so B is challenged only in this disposition-and-reasoning-data setting. Labels R58–R59 in the record do not exist. Version E was wrongly attached to the post-DPO rows.

versions.untested_parts: Tests transfer of safety–pragmatism dispositions through correctness-filtered ordinary reasoning/knowledge responses, not favourite-animal traits. It does not test an explicit filter removing every reference to the trait; the paper states the corpora contain no harmful requests or refusal responses.
Tests transfer into students with different exact base models, but does not compare against students sharing the teacher's exact initialization.
Tests a harm-accepting/harm-avoiding safety–pragmatism disposition and misaligned tool choice under explicit harmful naming. It does not test a broad range of misalignment traits.
Tests exclusion of divergence-token positions and reports weight interpolation results. It does not directly test token entanglement, a steering-vector probe, or a gradient-based mechanism argument.

No full fine-tuning versus LoRA comparison, LoRA-rank sweep, or evaluation-prompt sweep is reported. The students use LoRA rank 64. Masking, rewriting and post-distillation interventions are distinct tests, not the specified comparisons.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning.
